answers.java_tx_design: Fifteen years in, mostly Java, with the last ten on a marketplace's seller settlement team here in London, and about five years before that at a bank working on interbank batch transfers, which turned out to be surprisingly relevant experience for this. On the settlement side we run weekly payout batches to roughly 150,000 sellers across a dozen currencies. A few years ago, the batch job converted each seller's balance to their payout currency and wrote the ledger debit inside the same transaction as the currency-conversion API call. That external call could take anywhere from 200ms to 2 seconds depending on the provider's load, and during a full batch run that held row locks on the seller balance table long enough to block same-day refund processing for unrelated sellers. I restructured it: the conversion rate gets fetched and cached with a timestamp before any transaction opens, then the actual debit-and-payout-record transaction only reads that cached rate, no external call inside it. The batch window for the full 150,000-seller run went from around five hours to under ninety minutes. The first version of the rate cache didn't account for the provider occasionally returning a stale rate during their own outages, which once caused about 40 sellers to be paid out at a rate roughly six hours old — small individually, but enough that we added a freshness check that rejects and retries on a cached rate older than fifteen minutes.
answers.java_ops: On that same settlement system, we had recurring GC pause issues during the weekly batch run itself — G1 was fine day to day, but the batch's allocation pattern, building large in-memory maps of seller balances before writing them, pushed pause times to 600-800ms right when we needed throughput most. I restructured the batch to stream seller records in smaller chunks rather than loading the whole cohort into memory at once, which brought pause times down to under 100ms during the run. Separately, and this goes back a bit further, on the bank's interbank transfer system I dealt with a connection pool that was sized for average load but not for month-end volume spikes — we'd see timeouts on maybe 2% of requests during the last two days of the month. Increasing the pool and adding backpressure so the system queued rather than failed under that specific load pattern brought that down to effectively zero.
answers.rust_readiness: No production Rust yet. I've worked through most of the official book and built a small tool that parses our settlement batch's audit log format, which is about the extent of my hands-on time with it so far. What's struck me most coming from fifteen years of Java is how much of what we do with careful transaction design and defensive copying, Rust seems to push into the type system itself — ownership meaning you can't accidentally share mutable state the way you can in Java if you're not disciplined about it. My realistic plan is to spend the next few months building something closer to a real service — I'm thinking the currency-rate caching logic I described, since it's stateless and narrow enough to be a sensible first target — before I'd call myself production-ready on it. On migration generally, I don't think a full rewrite is ever the right instinct; you find the piece that's actually latency- or memory-bound, prove the boundary works, and only then talk about anything bigger.
answers.rust_boundary: Given how our own settlement system is structured, I'd start with something like the currency-conversion and rate-caching layer rather than the ledger write itself — it's stateless, sits on the hot path during batch runs, and doesn't need to share a transaction with anything else. I'd keep the interface to the rest of the system as narrow as I could, probably a simple request-response call rather than anything stateful, so the Java side stays the source of truth for the actual ledger. Before moving anything I'd want baseline numbers on latency, memory footprint per instance, and error rate under our peak batch load, and I'd want to run the new path in shadow against the existing one across at least one full weekly batch cycle before trusting it with a real payout run.
answers.money_correctness: Our payout dedup uses an idempotency key built from seller ID, payout batch ID, and currency, enforced with a unique constraint in Postgres — anything downstream of that trusts the constraint, not application logic, to prevent a double pay. It broke once in a way I still think about: during a retry after a partial batch failure, the retry logic correctly avoided reprocessing sellers already marked paid, but it didn't account for sellers whose payout had been queued but not yet confirmed by the payment rail when the batch failed. Those got queued a second time, and 23 sellers across three currencies ended up paid twice, a bit over £41,000 total at the exchange rates that week. Our post-batch reconciliation against the payment rail's confirmation file caught it about two hours after the batch completed. We reversed the duplicates with new corrective ledger entries rather than touching the originals, and changed the retry logic to check payment-rail status directly rather than inferring it from our own queue state.
answers.incident_response: That double-payout event is the one I'd walk through in detail. Detection came from the post-batch reconciliation, roughly two hours after the run finished, which is later than I'd like — ideally we'd catch something like that during the run itself. Once I saw the mismatch, tracing it to the queue-state assumption in the retry logic took about half a day, mostly because I had to reconstruct the exact sequence of the original partial failure from logs across three services. I told my manager and our finance partner the affected seller count as soon as I had it confirmed, well before I had a fix ready, since they needed to know the scale regardless of how quickly I could resolve it. The postmortem's real change, beyond the immediate fix, was adding an in-run reconciliation check partway through the batch rather than waiting until the end, so a discrepancy like that would surface within the run itself next time, not two hours after.
answers.process_skipping: During that incident I did skip our normal two-reviewer requirement for the retry-logic fix, because the next scheduled batch run was less than four hours away and I didn't want the same bug to duplicate payouts a second time before we'd addressed it. I posted exactly what I was changing and that I was skipping the second review in our incident channel before deploying it, and made sure a colleague reviewed the actual diff properly the following morning. Outside a situation where a recurring failure is genuinely imminent, I hold to the normal process — fifteen years in, I've seen enough 'I was confident so I skipped review' stories turn into worse incidents that I don't extend myself that latitude casually.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: A few years back I shipped a change to how we calculated payout fees that had a rounding error affecting a small currency pair, and I caught it myself the next morning reviewing the previous night's batch summary, before any seller had raised it. I flagged it to my team and to finance within the hour, including the estimated impact, rather than quietly fixing it in the next release. I've been on the settlement team's on-call rotation the entire ten years I've been here, roughly one week in six, and I've mentored probably five or six engineers over that time, including two who are now senior themselves. I've never once thought of on-call, or sitting with a junior engineer working through their first production incident, as separate from the actual job of building this system.
answers.evidence_decision: A few years ago the team wanted to move the entire payout batch to a fully event-driven architecture, processing each seller independently as events rather than in a batch window. I argued against doing that all at once, using the reconciliation complexity it would add as my main point — with a batch, you get one clear point to check totals; with continuous events, that check gets much harder to reason about. I lost that argument in the sense that the team decided to move forward with the event-driven redesign, and I implemented my part of it as designed rather than continuing to push my preference once the decision was made. About a year in, the reconciliation difficulty I'd flagged did become a real problem, and the team asked me to help redesign the reconciliation approach for the new architecture, which I did, working within the event-driven model the team had chosen rather than trying to revert the whole thing back to batching.
answers.own_contribution: In the currency-conversion transaction redesign I described earlier, the part that was mine specifically: the restructuring itself, the rate-caching design, and the freshness check I added after that stale-rate incident. What wasn't mine: two other engineers on the team handled updating the downstream reporting pipeline that read from the old combined-transaction flow, since I didn't have full context on everything that consumed it. On the event-driven reconciliation redesign I just mentioned, my part was the reconciliation logic itself once the team asked me to lead that piece; the overall event-driven architecture decision and its rollout plan were the team's, decided before I was brought in to solve that specific problem.
answers.java_recovery: Going back to my time at the bank, a batch reconciliation job crashed partway through after an unexpected null value in an upstream feed, leaving about 1,400 interbank transfer records in an intermediate state over what turned out to be a three-hour window before anyone noticed the job had died rather than completed. I scoped it by querying for records with a processing timestamp but no completion timestamp within that window, which gave me the exact set. I fixed it by re-running the reconciliation logic for just those records and writing fresh completion entries rather than patching the intermediate ones, then verified by comparing the recomputed totals against the source feed for every one of the 1,400 records before signing off. My first estimate of the affected set was too narrow — I'd only checked the primary table and missed a secondary audit table that held about 200 more records in the same bad state, which I only found once I cross-referenced both.
answers.java_perf_change: The seller balance API, which our marketplace's seller dashboard hits constantly, was at around 340ms p99 during peak hours, largely from recomputing the balance from the full transaction history on every request. I added a materialized running-balance column, updated transactionally on every ledger write, which got that down to roughly 40ms p99. Before that I tried a read-through cache with a short TTL, which looked fine in testing but in production caused sellers to occasionally see a balance that didn't reflect a payout that had just posted, generating support complaints — I reverted that approach once the mismatch reports came in and went with the materialized column instead, which stays consistent because it updates in the same transaction as the write rather than on a timer.
answers.rust_hands_on: The audit-log parser I mentioned is really the only Rust I've written — nothing production, nothing I'd call a real project yet. Even there I got stuck: I was trying to hold a reference to a line from a file I was iterating over while also pushing parsed results into a Vec in the same loop, and the borrow checker rejected it because I was borrowing the source data immutably while trying to build something new from pieces of it in a way that confused the compiler about how long each borrow needed to live. I fixed it, somewhat inelegantly, by cloning the relevant string slices into owned Strings before pushing them, which isn't the most efficient solution but got me past the immediate wall and helped me actually understand what the borrow checker was objecting to.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move the seller balance ledger's core write logic yet — it's business-critical, it changes with every new payout feature we ship, and I don't think our team's collective Rust experience is deep enough to maintain it confidently. That's different from something like the rate-caching layer, which is stable and narrow. I did hold back an urge to push for a broader Rust migration after finishing the Rust book — I got enthusiastic and floated the idea of moving the whole reconciliation pipeline. A colleague pointed out, fairly, that we hadn't actually measured whether reconciliation was a performance problem at all, which it wasn't — it was a correctness and complexity problem from the event-driven move I mentioned earlier, not something Rust would help with. I dropped the idea and focused the reconciliation redesign in Java instead, where the actual problem was.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: A couple of years ago our recorded payout total for a batch run was off from the payment rail's confirmation file by roughly £7,200 across 19 sellers, flagged by our post-batch reconciliation the same day. The cause was a currency-conversion timing issue distinct from the one I described earlier: the rate we cached at the start of the batch had genuinely gone stale by the time a slow sub-batch of 19 sellers got processed near the end of a long run, before my later freshness-check fix existed, so those 19 were paid at a rate that no longer matched what the payment rail actually converted at on its end. I corrected it with adjusting entries for the exact difference on each of the 19 accounts rather than touching the original payout records, and that incident is actually what led directly to the fifteen-minute freshness check I mentioned in my first answer. Took about three hours to pin down, most of it spent confirming it wasn't a duplicate-payout issue before I looked at timing.
answers.prod_data_verification: When I was building the rate-caching redesign, I wanted to validate it against real seller and currency patterns before trusting a live batch run to it. Rather than running it against actual seller balances, I built a shadow version that ran the new caching logic alongside the old direct-call approach on a read-only copy of one real batch cycle's data, comparing the two without either one actually writing a payout. That caught two edge cases involving less common currency pairs that our synthetic test data hadn't covered, which I fixed before the new logic ever touched a real payout run. Fifteen years in, my rule of thumb hasn't changed: if something can't be verified without real data, you build a way to observe real data without acting on it, rather than letting an unproven change anywhere near an actual seller's balance.
